abstract: Dr. Hadwen reviews the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) and tendon reflex techniques for hospital-based exams. He emphasizes the importance of standardized scoring to ensure inter-rater reliability, noting that a change of 3 or more points is clinically significant. Key teaching points include proper administration of level-of-consciousness questions (month and age), avoiding pantomime for command-following, and using binocular visual field testing to detect homonymous hemianopia. The talk also covers motor exam timing (10 seconds for arms, 5 seconds for legs) and scoring nuances for facial palsy and drift.
key_points: NIHSS has high inter-rater reliability; a change of 3 or more points warrants head imaging or rapid response.
For level of consciousness, ask only two standardized questions: month and age (not orientation to place).
When testing ability to follow commands, tell the patient to make a fist and close eyes, do not pantomime or place your fingers in their hand.
For visual fields, test binocularly with fists held 2, 2.5 feet away; flash fingers in upper and lower quadrants.
Extraocular movements are tested with horizontal gaze only; inability to cross midline scores 2 points.
Arms are held for 10 seconds, legs for 5 seconds; score 0 if no drift, 4 if no movement at all.
Facial palsy is scored by inspecting the nasolabial fold at rest and asking the patient to smile; lower-face weakness is typical for hemispheric stroke.
A score of 4 or more on initial NIHSS is considered disabling and may qualify for tPA.
Use MDCalc or a reference card to ensure accurate scoring, even experienced stroke neurologists do this.
Always perform NIHSS for any acute change in mental status, not just suspected stroke.
Motor testing should capture the patient's best effort by encouraging them during arm and leg holds.
Arm drift is assessed for 10 seconds, leg drift for 5 seconds, with the examiner helping position the leg initially.
